newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: E.Asian Grain - Korea, Taiwan seen buying corn.
newsitem.headline: E.Asian Grain - Korea, Taiwan seen buying corn.

text.p: South Korea and Taiwan are expected to buy more than 400,000 tonnes of corn this week to take advantage of a fall in prices, traders said on Monday.
The Koreans may buy 250,000 to 300,000 tonnes of Argentine corn while the Taiwanese would probably tender for at least 108,000 tonnes of corn, they said.
The Korea Feed Association is seeking 35,000 tonnes of feed corn and 15,000 tonnes of feed barley on Tuesday.

State-owned Taiwan Sugar Corp would probably tender for a combined shipment of 30,000 tonnes of U.S. corn and soybeans later this week, Taiwanese traders said. They said Members Feed Industry Group would seek a 54,000 tonne corn shipment for late November.
Taiwan's FGEP Group is also in the market for a 54,000 tonne corn shipment, although it has yet to decide on a delivery date.
But some traders said buyers were reluctant to fill their corn needs now as they expected prices to drop further.

"We expect corn prices to fall further because of last week's bearish USDA crop report and good crop weather in the U.S. We want to wait until prices fall further," a trader with Cheiljedang Corp in South Korea said.
The South Koreans are currently seeking Argentine corn for shipment next year, local traders said.
"Recently, our clients have begun frequently asking us for Argentine corn prices. They said it has a more attractive price and quality compared to U.S. corn," one trader said.
Seoul-based dealers said several local buyers were also seen ready to buy Canadian feed wheat instead of U.S. corn if the Canadian grain price was comparatively lower.
In Japan, lower freight rates on the U.S. Gulf/Japan route would make Japanese grain importers reluctant to buy U.S. corn and soybeans this week, local traders said.
"It's quiet. We're just watching import business by South Korea and Taiwan," a corn trader at a major trade house said.

Nearby freight rates on the U.S. Gulf/Japan route have fallen to below $20 a tonne from about $23 in June and $38 in May, mainly because newly-built Panamax-sized ships are entering the market, shipping industry officials said recently.
Some shipping firms quoted the rate at below $19 a tonne last week, they said.
"The freight is unlikely to fall further. But we'd like to confirm the bottom before buying U.S. grains," another corn trader said.
Japanese importers have already covered up to 60 percent of their January/March requirement for U.S. corn.
In the oilseeds market, Japanese importers have purchased nearly 30 percent of their U.S. soybean needs for November shipment and are unlikely to accelerate buying at this stage.
Delayed talks between crushers and feed makers over local soymeal prices for October/December 1996 deliveries have also held back purchasing, traders said.

Feed makers are concerned by the fall in Japanese animal feed demand caused by a decline in meat consumption following the O-157 colon bacillus food poisoning epidemic which has killed 11 people and made over 9,500 ill this year.
"There's still a wide gap between crushers and feed makers. But time is gradually running out, and they'll reach any compromise as early as next week," a soybean trader said.
"We'll return to the market after their agreement."
